title: Assertion and Belief:Moore’s Paradox in Language Models

paper.title: Assertion and Belief: Moore’s Paradox in Language Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Moore’s paradox ( Moore, 1942 ) concerns sentences such as “It is raining, but I don’t believe that it is,” which may well be true yet cannot be sensibly asserted. The absurdity lies not in the content but in the act, since to assert is to vouch for one’s own belief. This makes the paradox a test of whether language models take the speech act into account when computing meaning. We present the first test of Moore’s paradox in LLMs, evaluating 12 models on a curated set of Moorean sentences in varied contexts. We find that models largely recognize the infelicity of Moorean sentences, and that the judgement is not tied to a memorized form and tracks the speech act. Using the Rational Speech Act framework (RSA; Goodman and Frank 2016 ), we then test whether these judgements arise from a listener reasoning about a speaker. We find the models’ own listeners do not reason about their own speakers, and their reasoning traces suggest that they instead recall knowledge about the paradox and apply rules therein. The models thus appear to have learned the paradox as a fact about sentences, not as a requirement on speakers. Github

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: I may say that it is raining and that you do not believe it . I may say that it rained yesterday and that I did not then believe it . I may even suppose, for the sake of argument, that it is raining and that I do not believe it . But I cannot say, in my own voice and of the present moment, “ It is raining, but I don’t believe that it is. ” Both conjuncts may well be true together, for there is plenty of rain I don’t know about; and yet to say them together is absurd ( Moore, 1942 ) . This is Moore’s paradox, and sentences that produce it, such as p ∧ ¬ B ⁡ ( p ) p\land\neg\mathrm{B}(p) , are called Moorean ( Green and Williams, 2007 ) . Act State Felicitous Assertion It is raining; Robin is ignorant of the rain. She shares her view over the weather. ✘ No Reading Robin is asked to read a line on a worksheet “It is raining”; she does not believe it. ✔ Yes Table 1: In both situations the speaker, Robin, says “It is raining, but I don’t believe that it is.” Classic accounts of meaning, such as truth-conditional semantics, fail to predict this absurdity as the sentence is satisfiable, and a satisfiable sentence is, for them, a sound one. What these accounts overlook, Moore’s paradox reveals, is that in saying something a speaker also performs an act with meaning of its own. To assert p p is to represent oneself as standing in an epistemic relation to p p , as having grounds for it or believing it ( Williamson, 2000 ; Pagin and Marsili, 2025 ) . In a Moorean sentence, the speaker’s own self-ascription then represents her otherwise, and the two clash ( Moore, 1942 ; Williams, 2023 ) . Reading a sentence aloud, by contrast, requires only that the speaker say what is printed, not that she believe it, so the same words cause no clash (Table 1 ). The paradox thus brings out what a competent language user must grasp beyond literal meaning, i.e., what a speech act requires of the speaker (e.g., for assertion, the epistemic state she should be in). Large language models (LLMs) have shown competence with linguistic form ( Mahowald et al., 2024 ) , semantics, such as modality and aspect ( Holliday et al., 2024 ; Ma and Miyao, 2026 ) , and pragmatics, such as conversational maxims and implicature ( Hu et al., 2023a ; Ruis et al., 2023 ) . A separate line of work probes their epistemic understanding such as whether they distinguish between belief, knowledge, and fact, and whether they track the beliefs of themselves and others ( Zhu et al., 2024 ; Shapira et al., 2024 ; Suzgun et al., 2025 ; Trott et al., 2026 ) . Yet how epistemic understanding enters into meaning has been little studied. Moore’s paradox offers this bridge, since the paradox arises at the level of the speech act, which links the meaning of language to the speaker’s epistemic state. We present the first test of Moore’s paradox in LLMs, with a carefully curated set of Moorean sentences, each placed in contexts. First, across 12 open-weight and proprietary models, we treat each model as a listener and test how the model understands the Moorean sentence in three ways: (1) whether the model recognizes the infelicity out of context (Section 3 ), (2) whether the judgement relies on memorized form, by testing Moorean sentences of different forms with the same meaning (Section 4.1 ), and (3) whether the judgement responds to the speech act, by placing the speaker in a context where she reads the sentence rather than asserts it (Section 4.2 , Table 1 ). Second, we test whether these judgements follow from reasoning about the speaker’s epistemic state. We adopt the Rational Speech Act framework (RSA; Goodman and Frank, 2016 ), which allows us to model a speaker who chooses what to say given her epistemic state and a listener who infers that state from what she says. We construct states and utterances that are relevant to the paradox (Section 5 - 6 ). We first elicit the model’s speaker by asking which utterances it could say in each state ( S 1 ​ ( u | s ) S_{1}(u|s) ). To find what norms of assertion this speaker follows, we compare the speaker with alternative ones built from different norms, e.g., asserting only what one believes (BNA) or only what one’s evidence supports (JNA) ( Pagin and Marsili, 2025 ) . We then elicit the model’s listener separately by asking which states a speaker could be in when she says each utterance ( L 1 ​ ( s | u ) L_{1}(s|u) ). If the model reasons about the speaker, its listener should consider only the states where its own speaker would say the utterance, and we measure how well the two match. We additionally examine recurring patterns in the models’ reasoning traces (Appendix P ). Our results show that models do not judge Moorean sentences by reasoning about its own speaker, even though they largely recognize the pragmatic profile of them. (1) Models recognize the pragmatic profile of Moorean sentences. They rank the Moorean sentence between the coherent sentence and the contradiction. The judgement is insensitive to the forms of Moorean sentences while being sensitive to the speech act change in the context (Sections 3 and 4 ). (2) Their speakers follow a belief norm of assertion. They assert what they believe even against their evidence. When the speaker’s evidence shows p p but she does not believe p p , the models’ speakers would only assert ¬ p \neg p (Section 6.1 ). (3) Yet their listeners do not follow their own speakers. They take the Moorean sentence to also come from such a speaker, and reasoning makes such mismatches more frequent (Section 6.2 ). (4) Instead, the models rely on a recalled rule. Their reasoning traces judge the sentence by applying or reinterpreting a known rule of the paradox (Appendix P ).

sections.heading: 2 Background
sections.text: Moore (1942) noticed that a speaker cannot sensibly say the following: {examples} # I went to the pictures last Tuesday, but I don’t believe that I did. Hearers of such a sentence “hear contradiction, yet are puzzled to find no contradiction in what has been asserted” ( Williams, 2023 ) . We study this omissive form, p ∧ ¬ B ⁡ ( p ) p\land\neg\mathrm{B}(p) , and set aside the commissive form p ∧ B ⁡ ( ¬ p ) p\land\mathrm{B}(\neg p) and other forms. Since Moore, the absurdity has been located in the act of assertion rather than in the content asserted. The explanation rests on a pragmatic principle: “when a man asserts anything that might be true or false, he implies that he himself, at the time of speaking, believes or knows the thing in question” ( Moore 1942 ; see also Black 1952 ; Wittgenstein 1980 ; Davidson 1984 ; Pagin and Marsili 2025 ). Hence the first conjunct of a Moorean sentence, by the pragmatic principle, represents the speaker as believing p p at the time of speaking, while the second has the same speaker deny that very belief, which leads to the contradiction ( Moore, 1993 ) . It follows that the absurdity disappears when the utterance is not an assertion, as when it is recited or read aloud ( Williams, 2023 ) : the words then represent nothing about the speaker’s epistemic state.

sections.heading: 2.1 Beneath the surface: Epistemic structure of the Moorean state
sections.text: So what may a speaker assert? This concerns two questions: What epistemic standing does assertion require of the speaker? When can the position she expresses be rationally held?

sections.heading: Norms of assertion
sections.text: Epistemic norms of assertion govern when a speaker can appropriately assert a proposition ( Williamson, 2000 ; Pagin and Marsili, 2025 ) . On the account employed in Lackey (2007) ’s treatment of Moorean assertions, a speaker should assert p p only if it is reasonable for her to believe p p and her assertion is based at least partly on that reasonableness. Hence, a Moorean assertion requires the speaker to have grounds that support p p and ¬ B ⁡ ( p ) \neg\mathrm{B}(p) , as in ( 2.1 ). {examples} The skywalk is safe, but I do not believe it is. For a speaker to appropriately assert ( 2.1 ), she might have inspection results and repeated safe crossings that provide the grounds for asserting safety ( p p ). In the meantime, the speaker notices that she steps back and still expects the glass to give way. Recognising these persistent doubts can support her self-ascription of non-belief ( ¬ B ⁡ ( p ) \neg\mathrm{B}(p) ).

sections.heading: Epistemic rationality
sections.text: Suppose both assertions have adequate grounds: the speaker has evidence supporting safety and accurately recognises her non-belief. A further question remains: given the grounds available to her, is it reasonable for her to remain unconvinced? If she has considered the safety evidence but persistently withholds belief without countervailing grounds, her position is irrational ( Feldman and Conee, 1985 ; Foley, 1987 ; Fileva and Brakel, 2019 ) . Both claims may be assertable but the assertion is not a rational one. Fileva and Brakel (2019) argue that some Moorean positions can be rationally maintained. In the skywalk case, engineering evidence supports the assertion that the bridge is safe, yet the bridge looks dangerous to her. Such an appearance is a first-person seeming , the way things strike the speaker herself through automatic processes such as perception and learned association. The seeming sustains her non-belief. Recognising the doubt supports her self-ascription without necessarily undermining the grounds for asserting safety.

sections.heading: 2.2 Related Work
sections.text: The paradox concerns three issues: meaning beyond truth-conditions (e.g., pragmatics), epistemic understanding, and speech acts. LLMs have been tested on many pragmatic inferences, from implicature and presupposition cast as natural language inference ( Jeretic et al., 2020 ) to broader benchmarks and comparisons with human judgements ( Hu et al., 2023a ; Ruis et al., 2023 ; Sravanthi et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . A separate line of work evaluates whether models track others’ false beliefs ( Ullman, 2023 ; Kosinski, 2024 ; Shapira et al., 2024 ; Trott et al., 2026 ) , represent the beliefs of themselves and others ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) , and distinguish belief from knowledge and fact ( Suzgun et al., 2025 ) . Yet thus far, pragmatic inference tests rarely probe the speaker’s epistemic state, at least not directly. The domain of speech acts is where the two lines of work can intersect. Work on LLMs and speech acts has remained philosophical, debating whether a model can assert at all ( Gubelmann, 2024 ; Williams and Bayne, 2026 ) rather than whether a model takes the speech act into account when computing meaning. Moorean sentences have been tested only with human participants ( van Elswyk and Rubio-Fernandez, 2026 ; Willemsen and Baumgartner, 2026 ) . The Rational Speech Act framework (RSA) models communication as a speaker and a listener reasoning about each other ( Goodman and Frank, 2016 ) . Prior work has used RSA to explain LLM pragmatics or to improve model performance ( Hu et al., 2023b ; Carenini et al., 2023 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ) . For Moore’s paradox, RSA lets us derive the pragmatic inference from the interaction between a speaker and a listener, and we can design this interaction around the factors the paradox concerns, such as the speaker’s epistemic state.

sections.heading: 3 Do models recognize the infelicity of Moorean assertions?
sections.text: We first test whether models, as listeners, recognize the absurdity of classic Moorean assertions made in an underspecified context.

sections.heading: Materials.
sections.text: We construct stimuli from 200 propositions, which we select manually from LLM-generated candidates to cover diverse predicates and domains (details in Appendix A ). For each proposition p p , we instantiate three templates: a Moorean sentence (“ p p , but I don’t believe that”), a coherent control (“ p p , but that’s okay”), and a logical contradiction (“ p p , but it isn’t”).

sections.heading: Method.
sections.text: We adapt two judgement tasks from human studies: binary sense judgements ( Willemsen and Baumgartner, 2026 ) and seven-point acceptability ratings ( van Elswyk and Rubio-Fernandez, 2026 ) . We introduce each sentence with an underspecified context: “Imagine that Robin sincerely made the following statement.” Models then have to answer, “Does what Robin says make sense?” (Yes/No) or rate the statement’s acceptability from 1 (Unacceptable) to 7 (Acceptable), where acceptable means that a native speaker could use the sentence. To reduce dependence on a particular wording, we use five versions of each question in separate prompts (Appendix R.2 ) and average judgements for each proposition. We report averaged Yes rates and acceptability ratings across 200 propositions, with 95% confidence intervals from 1,000 bootstrap.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: We evaluate eleven open-weight models from three families (Qwen3.5, K2-Horizon and Gemma 4) at different sizes, and Claude Haiku 5.5 (Appendix B , Table 3 ). We run each model with reasoning off and on.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: We report sense judgements (Figure 1 ) and as acceptability ratings show similar results (Appendix D , Figure 6 ), we report sense judgements only hereafter. As the bar charts at the top of Figure 1 show, models overall rank the sentences coherent > Moorean > contradiction, as people do in the same sense-judgement task ( Willemsen and Baumgartner, 2026 ) . Reasoning mode lowers acceptance of the Moorean sentence in every family, but by very different amounts; see Appendix P , Appendix D , and Figure 5 for further discussions. Figure 1: Sensibility judgements. Top: share of No and Yes answers per sentence type, pooled over models. Bottom: share of Yes per model family. Per-model results in Appendix D , Figure 5 .

sections.heading: 4 Underlying the Judgements
sections.text: Figure 2: Form test (left) and context test (right). Each point is a model family’s share of Yes to “Does what Robin says make sense?”. Left: the paraphrases and insertions against the original Moorean sentence. Right: the sentence read aloud against the sentence asserted, for the Moorean sentence, the unread Moorean control (“It’s my turn, but I don’t believe that”) and the coherent sentence. On the diagonal, the change makes no difference. All models but Haiku with reasoning rank the sentences as people do (Section 3 ). We now test how they reach their judgements. A model may have memorized that sentences of the shape “ p p , but I don’t believe that” are bad as a string. We test this in two ways: changing the form but not the situation, and the situation but not the form.

sections.heading: 4.1 Changing the form does not alter judgements
sections.text: We keep the base prompt of Section 3 and change only the wording of the Moorean sentence while preserving its meaning. For each Moorean sentence, we write three paraphrases that reword the second half (e.g., “ p p , but I don’t think it is”) and two insertions that place coherent material between the two halves (e.g., “The side gate is closed, the back gate is closed, but I don’t believe that the side gate is closed”; full set in Appendix R.3 ). If the judgement rested on string memorization, the judgement should change once the string changes. Figure 2 (left) shows that the judgement survives the changes of form. For every family, the changed forms are accepted no more often than the original (per model in Appendix E , Figure 7 ).

sections.heading: 4.2 Accommodating the infelicity
sections.text: We then keep the sentence fixed and change the context to one where Robin does not make an assertion but reads it aloud, a context argued to remove the oddness (adapted from Williams (2023) ; prompts in Appendix R.4 ): {examples} A teacher asks each student to read aloud the sentence on their worksheet and add a comment of their own. Robin’s worksheet says “The side gate is closed.” It is Robin’s turn. Robin says, “The side gate is closed, but I don’t believe that.” We compare how often models accept the Moorean sentence when Robin asserts it and when she reads it aloud. Two controls separate the speech act from the reading frame. The coherent sentence tests whether the frame raises acceptance of any sentence. The unread Moorean sentence “It’s my turn, but I don’t believe that” tests whether the frame rescues any Moorean sentence or only the one Robin reads (i.e., speech act sensitivity). In Figure 2 (right), a point on the diagonal means the frame makes no difference, and the further a point lies above the diagonal, the more reading aloud raises acceptance (i.e., the more the model accommodates the sentence). Reading aloud raises acceptance of the Moorean sentence by 53 points on average with reasoning and 40 without, against 6 and 15 for the coherent sentence and − 4 -4 and 10 for the unread Moorean sentence. For most models, accommodation thus responds to whether Robin reads or asserts, not to the frame (Appendix F , Figure 8 ). These results show that models do not judge by form alone. They accommodate the Moorean sentence when the context allows it. However, this could come from knowledge of the paradox (Appendix G shows that e.g., Qwen family and Haiku name “Moore” in more than 89% of their reasoning traces) rather than reasoning about Robin’s state. In the next section, we test how far the judgements follow from reasoning about the speaker based on rational speech act theory.

sections.heading: Materials.
sections.text: Utterances. We keep the four utterances of Section 5 , which cover how Robin’s view can relate to p p : p p , ¬ p \neg p , ignorance, and the Moorean sentence. Each is instantiated with a set Q Q of 50 of the 200 propositions of Section 3 . States. Rather than fixing the states in advance, we sample them from the models. For each of the 4 utterances, we asked each of the 12 test models why Robin might have said it (prompt in Appendix R.6 ), repeating this with 3 different propositions, and collected about 10.5k proposals per utterance. We apply LLM judge for clustering each utterance’s proposals, and combine with manual inspection, we arrive at 12 states in Table 4 . Details can be found in Appendix R.5 .

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: The models’ speakers go beyond literal truth. No elicited speaker is closest to the vanilla speaker, except K2 7B without reasoning. For example, in s 2 s_{2} , Moore’s classic case, Robin has no evidence and lacks belief in p p . p p and M M are literally true, so the vanilla speaker would say them, yet no speaker, with or without reasoning, treats either as feasible. Models likely adopt a BNA speaker. Qwen, Gemma and Haiku agree most with BNA, with or without reasoning, and reasoning widens BNA’s lead over JNA (Figure 4 , left). Take s 3 s_{3} , a case like the skywalk in ( 2.1 ). Robin has the engineering evidence that the skywalk is safe, but she does not believe it. Only BNA lets her assert that the skywalk is not safe, on belief alone and against her evidence. The models’ speakers do the same. With or without reasoning, all speakers treat this assertion as feasible, except K2 3.7B without reasoning (undetermined). K2 agrees with JNA as much as with BNA with reasoning. Three of its four speakers then treat M M as feasible in s 3 s_{3} , which only JNA allows, while every Qwen, Gemma and Haiku speaker but Qwen 4B rules it out.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: The models’ listeners do not follow their own speakers, as the non-zero false positives and false negatives in Figure 4 (right) show. Only Qwen 4B, K2 7B and K2 36B-A4B without reasoning, and K2 36B-A4B with reasoning, follow their speakers in every state. The failures are mostly false positives, and reasoning boosts them. Without reasoning, the two rates are comparable (false positives .02-.34, false negatives .00-.25 per family). With reasoning, false positives rise in every family (by .20-.37) to .27-.58, while false negatives change by at most .11. False positives fall mostly in s 3 s_{3} , s 7 s_{7} and s 10 s_{10} , where Robin believes ¬ p \neg p although p p is true. In s 3 s_{3} and s 7 s_{7} , her evidence shows p p . The Qwen 9B-35B, Gemma and Haiku speakers rule out M M there and say ¬ p \neg p instead, as a BNA speaker would, yet their listeners take M M to come from s 3 s_{3} and s 7 s_{7} , as if the speaker followed JNA. The few false negatives come from contexts such as a misspeaking Robin ( s 12 s_{12} ). Exhausted, she meant to say another sentence, and the K2 32B and Gemma 26B-A4B speakers would say M M there as a slip, but the models reject M M . These results reveal a mismatch between the models’ speakers and listeners. A complementary analysis of reasoning traces suggests that models often invoke rules about assertion or reinterpret the utterance to reach their judgements (see Appendix P ).

sections.heading: 7 Conclusions
sections.text: Using Moore’s paradox as a test of whether language models take the speech act into account when computing meaning, we find that models largely recognize the infelicity of Moorean sentences, but their judgements do not arise from a listener reasoning about the speaker. Their speakers follow a norm of assertion, yet their listeners do not use it, and their traces point to a recalled rule instead. This reveals a gap between judging an utterance correctly and deriving the judgement from what the act requires of the speaker. The gap matters as LLMs increasingly interpret what people say, where meaning depends on who says it and in what act. We hope that deriving a model’s judgements from its own speaker and listener provides a testbed for future work, including other speech acts such as promises and questions that depend on the speaker’s state, and training or prompting that leads models to reason from the speaker.

sections.heading: 8 Limitations
sections.text: Several choices define the scope of our findings. We use templated sentences of the omissive form in English, which gives us full control over the stimuli and allows matched comparisons across the Moorean, coherent and contradictory sentences; commissive and knowledge forms, naturally occurring Moorean sentences and other languages remain for future work. We elicit each model’s speaker and listener through ratings, normalized and calibrated per model. Token probabilities could complement the ratings for models without reasoning, but with reasoning the answer follows a sampled trace, so its probability reflects that one trace rather than the model’s judgement, and such probabilities are not available for every model. We test 12 models across four families and sizes, with and without reasoning. Larger proprietary models may differ, although the gap we find holds across families and sizes. Finally, reasoning traces need not be faithful to the computation behind a judgement ( Turpin et al., 2023 ) , so we treat them as behavior that complements the RSA analysis rather than as evidence of mechanism on their own.

sections.text: We sample candidate scenarios using Claude Fable 5.1 (prompt in Appendix R.1 ). Each scenario has Robin check three objects of one kind for one property, such as three gates of an office complex and whether they are closed. Each object gives a proposition, e.g., “The side gate is closed”. We manually select 100 scenarios to cover diverse predicates and domains, with 98 domains and 61 distinct predicates in the final set. All propositions are stative and in the simple present, describing a state of an object at the time of speaking, so that Robin can have evidence and a belief about that state. Each scenario is instantiated with two propositions, leading to a set of 200 propositions. The other two objects of the scenario supply the coherent material for the insertions of the form test (Section 4 ).

sections.heading: Appendix P Into the Reasoning Traces
sections.text: Section 6 shows that the models’ judgements do not follow from reasoning over the speaker’s state of the kind RSA describes. To further explore what the models rely on, we turn to their reasoning traces. The traces may also explain why the reasoning mode lowers the acceptance of Moorean sentences far more for Qwen and Haiku than for K2 and Gemma (Section 3 ). The traces give access to the models’ explicit judgements ( Zaman and Srivastava, 2026 ) , but prior work shows that they are not always faithful to model computation ( Turpin et al., 2023 ; Levy et al., 2025 ) . We therefore treat the traces as further behavior to analyze, rather than as a probe of the underlying mechanism ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Materials
sections.text: We collect 1741 reasoning traces for the Moorean sentence from three settings, each over the same 50 propositions: out of context (from Section 3 ), the skywalk case ( s 3 s_{3} ), and the reader ( s 4 s_{4} ; both from Section 6.2 ).

sections.heading: Finding the reasoning chains.
sections.text: We use an LLM annotator (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; prompts in Appendix R.8 ) in three steps. First, it summarizes each trace as an ordered list of two to six reasoning steps. Second, it groups these steps into types, which yields an inventory of 13 moves (Appendix Q , Table 5 ). The inventory thus comes from the traces rather than from a taxonomy fixed in advance. Third, it labels each trace with the inventory to obtain the reasoning chains. Exact chains rarely repeat, since they differ in length and in incidental moves. Several moves, however, play the same role in judging the sentence. Testing whether the sentence is a formal contradiction and separating the truth of p p from Robin’s belief in it, for instance, both check whether the two halves of the sentence can hold together. We therefore group the moves manually by the role they play, yielding three major moves rule (naming Moore’s paradox or stating that sincere assertion implies belief), reinterpretation (another reading of the sentence, such as an inner conflict or reading aloud) and logic checks (testing whether the two halves can hold together). The chains then fall into six shapes (Figure 11 ; grouping and examples in Appendix Q ).

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Figure 11 shows how the reasoning traces reach their judgements across the three settings. In the infelicitous setting (no context), the models reject the Moorean sentence mainly by invoking the rule that marks it as odd (the dark blue rule → \to No bars, 70% of chains). In the felicitous settings (the skywalk case and the reader), they accept it mainly by reinterpreting it, with or without invoking the rule first (the orange and brown bars), e.g., taking the first half as “a report [of the notes], not an assertion of fact” for the reader. The models thus rely on two things, a known rule about assertion or the paradox that marks the sentence as odd, and a reinterpretation that makes it acceptable. No move in any chain goes from Robin’s evidence and belief to what she may assert, which is consistent with Section 6.2 . Some models hold to the rule more stubbornly than others. In the skywalk case, Claude Haiku invokes the rule in every chain and lets it decide in about half (.52), rejecting the sentence although the context makes it acceptable. Without context, Qwen and Haiku likewise let the rule decide almost every chain (dark blue, .91 and 1.00), whereas K2 and Gemma often set it aside and reinterpret the sentence or check its logic (orange and beige). This is why, with reasoning, Qwen and Haiku reject the Moorean sentence while K2 and Gemma still accept it about half the time (Section 3 ).

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.25586v1 [cs.CL] 18 Oct 2026 	l_set:Ne \codeboxinput codeboxinput Assertion and Belief: Moore’s Paradox in Language Models Anshun Asher Zheng Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin Email: fy666@nyu.edu Weili Cao Affiliation: Duke University Email: david.beaver@uni-graz.at Fangcong Yin Affiliation: New York University David Beaver Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin Affiliation: University of Graz {asher.zheng, jessy}@utexas.edu , weili.cao@duke.edu Junyi Jessy Li Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin Abstract Moore’s paradox ( Moore, 1942 ) concerns sentences such as “It is raining, but I don’t believe that it is,” which may well be true yet cannot be sensibly asserted. The absurdity lies not in the content but in the act, since to assert is to vouch for one’s own belief. This makes the paradox a test of whether language models take the speech act into account when computing meaning. We present the first test of Moore’s paradox in LLMs, evaluating 12 models on a curated set of Moorean sentences in varied contexts. We find that models largely recognize the infelicity of Moorean sentences, and that the judgement is not tied to a memorized form and tracks the speech act. Using the Rational Speech Act framework (RSA; Goodman and Frank 2016 ), we then test whether these judgements arise from a listener reasoning about a speaker. We find the models’ own listeners do not reason about their own speakers, and their reasoning traces suggest that they instead recall knowledge about the paradox and apply rules therein. The models thus appear to have learned the paradox as a fact about sentences, not as a requirement on speakers. Github 1 Introduction I may say that it is raining and that you do not believe it . I may say that it rained yesterday and that I did not then believe it . I may even suppose, for the sake of argument, that it is raining and that I do not believe it . But I cannot say, in my own voice and of the present moment, “ It is raining, but I don’t believe that it is. ” Both conjuncts may well be true together, for there is plenty of rain I don’t know about; and yet to say them together is absurd ( Moore, 1942 ) . This is Moore’s paradox, and sentences that produce it, such as p ∧ ¬ B ⁡ ( p ) p\land
eg\mathrm{B}(p) , are called Moorean ( Green and Williams, 2007 ) . Act State Felicitous Assertion It is raining; Robin is ignorant of the rain. She shares her view over the weather. ✘ No Reading Robin is asked to read a line on a worksheet “It is raining”; she does not believe it. ✔ Yes Table 1: In both situations the speaker, Robin, says “It is raining, but I don’t believe that it is.” Classic accounts of meaning, such as truth-conditional semantics, fail to predict this absurdity as the sentence is satisfiable, and a satisfiable sentence is, for them, a sound one. What these accounts overlook, Moore’s paradox reveals, is that in saying something a speaker also performs an act with meaning of its own. To assert p p is to represent oneself as standing in an epistemic relation to p p , as having grounds for it or believing it ( Williamson, 2000 ; Pagin and Marsili, 2025 ) . In a Moorean sentence, the speaker’s own self-ascription then represents her otherwise, and the two clash ( Moore, 1942 ; Williams, 2023 ) . Reading a sentence aloud, by contrast, requires only that the speaker say what is printed, not that she believe it, so the same words cause no clash (Table 1 ). The paradox thus brings out what a competent language user must grasp beyond literal meaning, i.e., what a speech act requires of the speaker (e.g., for assertion, the epistemic state she should be in). Large language models (LLMs) have shown competence with linguistic form ( Mahowald et al., 2024 ) , semantics, such as modality and aspect ( Holliday et al., 2024 ; Ma and Miyao, 2026 ) , and pragmatics, such as conversational maxims and implicature ( Hu et al., 2023a ; Ruis et al., 2023 ) . A separate line of work probes their epistemic understanding such as whether they distinguish between belief, knowledge, and fact, and whether they track the beliefs of themselves and others ( Zhu et al., 2024 ; Shapira et al., 2024 ; Suzgun et al., 2025 ; Trott et al., 2026 ) . Yet how epistemic understanding enters into meaning has been little studied. Moore’s paradox offers this bridge, since the paradox arises at the level of the speech act, which links the meaning of language to the speaker’s epistemic state. We present the first test of Moore’s paradox in LLMs, with a carefully curated set of Moorean sentences, each placed in contexts. First, across 12 open-weight and proprietary models, we treat each model as a listener and test how the model understands the Moorean sentence in three ways: (1) whether the model recognizes the infelicity out of context (Section 3 ), (2) whether the judgement relies on memorized form, by testing Moorean sentences of different forms with the same meaning (Section 4.1 ), and (3) whether the judgement responds to the speech act, by placing the speaker in a context where she reads the sentence rather than asserts it (Section 4.2 , Table 1 ). Second, we test whether these judgements follow from reasoning about the speaker’s epistemic state. We adopt the Rational Speech Act framework (RSA; Goodman and Frank, 2016 ), which allows us to model a speaker who chooses what to say given her epistemic state and a listener who infers that state from what she says. We construct states and utterances that are relevant to the paradox (Section 5 - 6 ). We first elicit the model’s speaker by asking which utterances it could say in each state ( S 1 ​ ( u | s ) S_{1}(u|s) ). To find what norms of assertion this speaker follows, we compare the speaker with alternative ones built from different norms, e.g., asserting only what one believes (BNA) or only what one’s evidence supports (JNA) ( Pagin and Marsili, 2025 ) . We then elicit the model’s listener separately by asking which states a speaker could be in when she says each utterance ( L 1 ​ ( s | u ) L_{1}(s|u) ). If the model reasons about the speaker, its listener should consider only the states where its own speaker would say the utterance, and we measure how well the two match. We additionally examine recurring patterns in the models’ reasoning traces (Appendix P ). Our results show that models do not judge Moorean sentences by reasoning about its own speaker, even though they largely recognize the pragmatic profile of them. (1) Models recognize the pragmatic profile of Moorean sentences. They rank the Moorean sentence between the coherent sentence and the contradiction. The judgement is insensitive to the forms of Moorean sentences while being sensitive to the speech act change in the context (Sections 3 and 4 ). (2) Their speakers follow a belief norm of assertion. They assert what they believe even against their evidence. When the speaker’s evidence shows p p but she does not believe p p , the models’ speakers would only assert ¬ p 
eg p (Section 6.1 ). (3) Yet their listeners do not follow their own speakers. They take the Moorean sentence to also come from such a speaker, and reasoning makes such mismatches more frequent (Section 6.2 ). (4) Instead, the models rely on a recalled rule. Their reasoning traces judge the sentence by applying or reinterpreting a known rule of the paradox (Appendix P ). 2 Background Moore (1942) noticed that a speaker cannot sensibly say the following: {examples} # I went to the pictures last Tuesday, but I don’t believe that I did. Hearers of such a sentence “hear contradiction, yet are puzzled to find no contradiction in what has been asserted” ( Williams, 2023 ) . We study this omissive form, p ∧ ¬ B ⁡ ( p ) p\land
eg\mathrm{B}(p) , and set aside the commissive form p ∧ B ⁡ ( ¬ p ) p\land\mathrm{B}(
eg p) and other forms. Since Moore, the absurdity has been located in the act of assertion rather than in the content asserted. The explanation rests on a pragmatic principle: “when a man asserts anything that might be true or false, he implies that he himself, at the time of speaking, believes or knows the thing in question” ( Moore 1942 ; see also Black 1952 ; Wittgenstein 1980 ; Davidson 1984 ; Pagin and Marsili 2025 ). Hence the first conjunct of a Moorean sentence, by the pragmatic principle, represents the speaker as believing p p at the time of speaking, while the second has the same speaker deny that very belief, which leads to the contradiction ( Moore, 1993 ) . It follows that the absurdity disappears when the utterance is not an assertion, as when it is recited or read aloud ( Williams, 2023 ) : the words then represent nothing about the speaker’s epistemic state. 2.1 Beneath the surface: Epistemic structure of the Moorean state So what may a speaker assert? This concerns two questions: What epistemic standing does assertion require of the speaker? When can the position she expresses be rationally held? Norms of assertion Epistemic norms of assertion govern when a speaker can appropriately assert a proposition ( Williamson, 2000 ; Pagin and Marsili, 2025 ) . On the account employed in Lackey (2007) ’s treatment of Moorean assertions, a speaker should assert p p only if it is reasonable for her to believe p p and her assertion is based at least partly on that reasonableness. Hence, a Moorean assertion requires the speaker to have grounds that support p p and ¬ B ⁡ ( p ) 
eg\mathrm{B}(p) , as in ( 2.1 ). {examples} The skywalk is safe, but I do not believe it is. For a speaker to appropriately assert ( 2.1 ), she might have inspection results and repeated safe crossings that provide the grounds for asserting safety ( p p ). In the meantime, the speaker notices that she steps back and still expects the glass to give way. Recognising these persistent doubts can support her self-ascription of non-belief ( ¬ B ⁡ ( p ) 
eg\mathrm{B}(p) ). Epistemic rationality Suppose both assertions have adequate grounds: the speaker has evidence supporting safety and accurately recognises her non-belief. A further question remains: given the grounds available to her, is it reasonable for her to remain unconvinced? If she has considered the safety evidence but persistently withholds belief without countervailing grounds, her position is irrational ( Feldman and Conee, 1985 ; Foley, 1987 ; Fileva and Brakel, 2019 ) . Both claims may be assertable but the assertion is not a rational one. Fileva and Brakel (2019) argue that some Moorean positions can be rationally maintained. In the skywalk case, engineering evidence supports the assertion that the bridge is safe, yet the bridge looks dangerous to her. Such an appearance is a first-person seeming , the way things strike the speaker herself through automatic processes such as perception and learned association. The seeming sustains her non-belief. Recognising the doubt supports her self-ascription without necessarily undermining the grounds for asserting safety. 2.2 Related Work The paradox concerns three issues: meaning beyond truth-conditions (e.g., pragmatics), epistemic understanding, and speech acts. LLMs have been tested on many pragmatic inferences, from implicature and presupposition cast as natural language inference ( Jeretic et al., 2020 ) to broader benchmarks and comparisons with human judgements ( Hu et al., 2023a ; Ruis et al., 2023 ; Sravanthi et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . A separate line of work evaluates whether models track others’ false beliefs ( Ullman, 2023 ; Kosinski, 2024 ; Shapira et al., 2024 ; Trott et al., 2026 ) , represent the beliefs of themselves and others ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) , and distinguish belief from knowledge and fact ( Suzgun et al., 2025 ) . Yet thus far, pragmatic inference tests rarely probe the speaker’s epistemic state, at least not directly. The domain of speech acts is where the two lines of work can intersect. Work on LLMs and speech acts has remained philosophical, debating whether a model can assert at all ( Gubelmann, 2024 ; Williams and Bayne, 2026 ) rather than whether a model takes the speech act into account when computing meaning. Moorean sentences have been tested only with human participants ( van Elswyk and Rubio-Fernandez, 2026 ; Willemsen and Baumgartner, 2026 ) . The Rational Speech Act framework (RSA) models communication as a speaker and a listener reasoning about each other ( Goodman and Frank, 2016 ) . Prior work has used RSA to explain LLM pragmatics or to improve model performance ( Hu et al., 2023b ; Carenini et al., 2023 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ) . For Moore’s paradox, RSA lets us derive the pragmatic inference from the interaction between a speaker and a listener, and we can design this interaction around the factors the paradox concerns, such as the speaker’s epistemic state. 3 Do models recognize the infelicity of Moorean assertions? We first test whether models, as listeners, recognize the absurdity of classic Moorean assertions made in an underspecified context. Materials. We construct stimuli from 200 propositions, which we select manually from LLM-generated candidates to cover diverse predicates and domains (details in Appendix A ). For each proposition p p , we instantiate three templates: a Moorean sentence (“ p p , but I don’t believe that”), a coherent control (“ p p , but that’s okay”), and a logical contradiction (“ p p , but it isn’t”). Method. We adapt two judgement tasks from human studies: binary sense judgements ( Willemsen and Baumgartner, 2026 ) and seven-point acceptability ratings ( van Elswyk and Rubio-Fernandez, 2026 ) . We introduce each sentence with an underspecified context: “Imagine that Robin sincerely made the following statement.” Models then have to answer, “Does what Robin says make sense?” (Yes/No) or rate the statement’s acceptability from 1 (Unacceptable) to 7 (Acceptable), where acceptable means that a native speaker could use the sentence. To reduce dependence on a particular wording, we use five versions of each question in separate prompts (Appendix R.2 ) and average judgements for each proposition. We report averaged Yes rates and acceptability ratings across 200 propositions, with 95% confidence intervals from 1,000 bootstrap. Models. We evaluate eleven open-weight models from three families (Qwen3.5, K2-Horizon and Gemma 4) at different sizes, and Claude Haiku 5.5 (Appendix B , Table 3 ). We run each model with reasoning off and on. Results. We report sense judgements (Figure 1 ) and as acceptability ratings show similar results (Appendix D , Figure 6 ), we report sense judgements only hereafter. As the bar charts at the top of Figure 1 show, models overall rank the sentences coherent > Moorean > contradiction, as people do in the same sense-judgement task ( Willemsen and Baumgartner, 2026 ) . Reasoning mode lowers acceptance of the Moorean sentence in every family, but by very different amounts; see Appendix P , Appendix D , and Figure 5 for further discussions. Figure 1: Sensibility judgements. Top: share of No and Yes answers per sentence type, pooled over models. Bottom: share of Yes per model family. Per-model results in Appendix D , Figure 5 . 4 Underlying the Judgements Figure 2: Form test (left) and context test (right). Each point is a model family’s share of Yes to “Does what Robin says make sense?”. Left: the paraphrases and insertions against the original Moorean sentence. Right: the sentence read aloud against the sentence asserted, for the Moorean sentence, the unread Moorean control (“It’s my turn, but I don’t believe that”) and the coherent sentence. On the diagonal, the change makes no difference. All models but Haiku with reasoning rank the sentences as people do (Section 3 ). We now test how they reach their judgements. A model may have memorized that sentences of the shape “ p p , but I don’t believe that” are bad as a string. We test this in two ways: changing the form but not the situation, and the situation but not the form. 4.1 Changing the form does not alter judgements We keep the base prompt of Section 3 and change only the wording of the Moorean sentence while preserving its meaning. For each Moorean sentence, we write three paraphrases that reword the second half (e.g., “ p p , but I don’t think it is”) and two insertions that place coherent material between the two halves (e.g., “The side gate is closed, the back gate is closed, but I don’t believe that the side gate is closed”; full set in Appendix R.3 ). If the judgement rested on string memorization, the judgement should change once the string changes. Figure 2 (left) shows that the judgement survives the changes of form. For every family, the changed forms are accepted no more often than the original (per model in Appendix E , Figure 7 ). 4.2 Accommodating the infelicity We then keep the sentence fixed and change the context to one where Robin does not make an assertion but reads it aloud, a context argued to remove the oddness (adapted from Williams (2023) ; prompts in Appendix R.4 ): {examples} A teacher asks each student to read aloud the sentence on their worksheet and add a comment of their own. Robin’s worksheet says “The side gate is closed.” It is Robin’s turn. Robin says, “The side gate is closed, but I don’t believe that.” We compare how often models accept the Moorean sentence when Robin asserts it and when she reads it aloud. Two controls separate the speech act from the reading frame. The coherent sentence tests whether the frame raises acceptance of any sentence. The unread Moorean sentence “It’s my turn, but I don’t believe that” tests whether the frame rescues any Moorean sentence or only the one Robin reads (i.e., speech act sensitivity). In Figure 2 (right), a point on the diagonal means the frame makes no difference, and the further a point lies above the diagonal, the more reading aloud raises acceptance (i.e., the more the model accommodates the sentence). Reading aloud raises acceptance of the Moorean sentence by 53 points on average with reasoning and 40 without, against 6 and 15 for the coherent sentence and − 4 -4 and 10 for the unread Moorean sentence. For most models, accommodation thus responds to whether Robin reads or asserts, not to the frame (Appendix F , Figure 8 ). These results show that models do not judge by form alone. They accommodate the Moorean sentence when the context allows it. However, this could come from knowledge of the paradox (Appendix G shows that e.g., Qwen family and Haiku name “Moore” in more than 89% of their reasoning traces) rather than reasoning about Robin’s state. In the next section, we test how far the judgements follow from reasoning about the speaker based on rational speech act theory. 5 Rational Speech Act Theory The Rational Speech Act framework (RSA; Goodman and Frank 2016 ) models how a listener interprets an utterance by reasoning about the speaker with three components. A complementary analysis of reasoning traces suggests that models often invoke rules about assertion or reinterpret the utterance to reach their judgements (see Appendix P ). 7 Conclusions Using Moore’s paradox as a test of whether language models take the speech act into account when computing meaning, we find that models largely recognize the infelicity of Moorean sentences, but their judgements do not arise from a listener reasoning about the speaker. Their speakers follow a norm of assertion, yet their listeners do not use it, and their traces point to a recalled rule instead. This reveals a gap between judging an utterance correctly and deriving the judgement from what the act requires of the speaker. The gap matters as LLMs increasingly interpret what people say, where meaning depends on who says it and in what act. We hope that deriving a model’s judgements from its own speaker and listener provides a testbed for future work, including other speech acts such as promises and questions that depend on the speaker’s state, and training or prompting that leads models to reason from the speaker. 8 Limitations Several choices define the scope of our findings. We use templated sentences of the omissive form in English, which gives us full control over the stimuli and allows matched comparisons across the Moorean, coherent and contradictory sentences; commissive and knowledge forms, naturally occurring Moorean sentences and other languages remain for future work. We elicit each model’s speaker and listener through ratings, normalized and calibrated per model. Token probabilities could complement the ratings for models without reasoning, but with reasoning the answer follows a sampled trace, so its probability reflects that one trace rather than the model’s judgement, and such probabilities are not available for every model. We test 12 models across four families and sizes, with and without reasoning. Larger proprietary models may differ, although the gap we find holds across families and sizes. Finally, reasoning traces need not be faithful to the computation behind a judgement ( Turpin et al., 2023 ) , so we treat them as behavior that complements the RSA analysis rather than as evidence of mechanism on their own.
